question: After Rome, which fats survive where — and what do cooks, monks, stewards and herders keep going?
thesis: Rome’s collapse doesn’t erase a fat economy, it splits one into pieces that stop talking to each other. The Latin north builds its own world of butter, pork and whale from the ruins, with only the Church keeping a Mediterranean habit alive as a rite. The Islamic world does not inherit Rome’s oil — it continues a Near Eastern, Persian-rooted fat culture older than Rome, intellectualizes it into a medicine of the humours, and pushes its own vocabulary for oil into Iberia. And the same outside force, Buddhism, does different things in different places: it empties Japan’s kitchen of fat for good, because Japan had no herds to put it back with; it leaves South India’s much older ghee economy largely untouched; and at the Tang court it is joined by something new — the ruling house’s own Turkic ancestry, which makes dairy fat fashionable for the first time.

big_ideas.title: Rome’s collapse splits Europe, not just empties it
big_ideas.text: The Latin north builds its own animal-fat economy from the ruins — Anglo-Saxon and Irish butter, Frankish accounts, pannage, Norse whaling, Icelandic whale-feuds — and even its soap craft divides along the old oil line, tallow in the north, olive oil in Italy. The Church keeps one Mediterranean habit alive, but only as a rite, in holy oils and altar lamps.

big_ideas.title: Islam continues an older fat culture, and exports it
big_ideas.text: Tail fat, sesame and olive oil in the Baghdad cookbook are not Roman survivals — tail fat was already prized in the pre-Islamic Near East, sesame is Persian and Indian, and the cookbook’s humoral judgments (butter ‘floats at the stomach’s mouth’) are its own. The Prophet inherits a shared Abrahamic reverence for oil, Iran’s own sesame economy continues, and Arabic rule reshapes the very words Iberia uses for oil.

big_ideas.title: Buddhism reaches three regions and does three different things
big_ideas.text: In Tang monasteries an oil lamp must never go out, and a Buddhist ladder ranks milk through to the refined ti-hu. In Japan, Emperor Temmu’s ban — usually read as Buddhist, though Ishige adds fear for a sparse animal stock — becomes permanent only because Japan never had herds to bring fat back with. In South India the much older Vedic ghee-for-lamps tradition simply continues, now paid for by Chola temple endowments instead of household sacrifice.

big_ideas.title: Foreign tastes remake Tang taste, Turkic and Persian alike
big_ideas.text: Dairy fat reaches its peak in China under a Tang ruling house of part-Turkic ancestry, which gives an old northern frontier practice new status at court. Baghdad’s own dairy needs no such story: its yogurt preparations trace back to Akkadian Mesopotamia, already ancient and ordinary centuries before any Turkic contact. Iranian vendors sell sesame-oil-fried cakes on the capital’s street corners at the same time — a separate, trade-driven foreign influence, not the ruling house’s own.

threads.title: Rome’s collapse splits Europe: the Latin north builds its own economy
threads.claim: The north does not lose a Roman inheritance so much as build a new animal-fat economy from the ruins, with the Church keeping one Mediterranean habit as a rite.

beats.text: Butter in Anglo-Saxon England comes from ewes’ milk and is a lord’s luxury.
Pigs are pastured in the forest on the autumn mast, and mast rights outweigh timber as forest income.
The Capitulary De Villis tells royal stewards to account for fat, tallow, butter and soap.
Irish butter is buried in the peat in wooden firkins and bladders.
Ohthere describes hunting whales and walrus on the White Sea; whaling is certain in the North Sea by the 800s.
In the Icelandic sagas families fight over the ownership of whale carcasses.
Soap is a craft by now, above all in Italy, its fat split the same way the continent’s is: tallow in the north, olive oil in the Mediterranean.
Monasteries and cathedrals remain islands of oil expertise for holy oils and church lamps.

threads.title: Islam continues an older Near Eastern fat culture, and exports it
threads.claim: None of this is Rome’s: tail fat, sesame and olive oil are older than the empire that just fell, and the Islamic world both intellectualizes them and pushes its own vocabulary for oil into formerly-Roman Iberia.

beats.text: In tradition the Prophet uses so much olive oil that his shawl is often drenched with it.
Meat is first fried in rendered sheep’s tail fat, ‘sweated’ to remove bad odours.
Bread is rubbed with sesame oil or the oil of unripe olives before it meets the oven wall.
Fats are weighed by their effect on the humours: butter floats at the stomach’s mouth, clarified butter does not.
Abu Mansur names sesame as a crop of Iran.
Spanish aceite and aceituna come from Andalusi Arabic az-zayt and az-zaytūna.

threads.title: Buddhism reaches three regions, with three results
threads.claim: The same religious wave touches Tang China, Japan and South India, and produces a different fat story in each, because of what economy it met.

beats.text: An oil lamp that is never allowed to go out is a symbol in Tang monasteries.
The Tang pharmacopoeia sets a ladder of milk, soured milk, su and ti hu as the stages of the soul.

Emperor Temmu bans beef, horse, dog, monkey and chicken in the farming months, on pain of execution — usually read as Buddhist, though Ishige notes it may also reflect fear for an already sparse animal stock.
Japan cooks almost without oil or fat at all: with no systematic herding, once the taboo took hold there was no economy to bring animal fat back with.
Tamil texts describe the sesame press, the chekku, and sesame oil is exported from the south.
Chola temples are given flocks of 90 to 96 sheep to supply ghee for a perpetual lamp.

threads.title: The Tang court draws in foreign tastes, Turkic and Persian alike
threads.claim: Dairy fat becomes fashionable because the ruling house has Turkic ancestry; a separate, trade-driven channel brings Persian frying oil to the capital’s streets at the same time.

beats.text: Cream, yogurt, cheese and butter are popular, a climax of Chinese dairy fat.
Pharmacologists argue whether cow or goat kaymak is better, and it goes into banquet pastries.
Iranian vendors sell sesame-oil cakes on Tang street corners — a different, trade-driven foreign influence, not the ruling house’s own.

turning_points.text: Anglo-Saxon butter and Irish bog butter mark the north’s own dairy economy.
The Prophet’s olive-oil tradition inherits a shared Abrahamic reverence for oil.
Emperor Temmu bans meat eating in the farming months.
Dairy fat reaches its peak in China under the part-Turkic Tang.
The Tang pharmacopoeia fixes the Buddhist ladder from milk to ti-hu.
Spanish takes its oil words from Arabic.
Frankish stewards must account for fat, tallow and soap.
Ohthere hunts whales and walrus on the White Sea.
Chola temples endow lamps with flocks of sheep for ghee.
The Baghdad cookbook puts tail fat and oil in the pot, and judges both by the humours.
Abu Mansur names sesame as a crop of Iran.

text: Nine entries, from the Frankish estates to the Irish bogs: the north’s fat is butter, tallow and soap, kept by stewards, hidden against raiders, fought over when a whale strands, and pork fat fed on the autumn mast of the forest ([[o1]], [[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[c1]], [[ec5]], [[ec10]]); the church and Arabic keep the Mediterranean’s oil in the picture ([[b1]], [[th1]], [[ec4]]).

Baghdad and the Prophet: cooking, dietetics and an oil anecdote ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]], [[b4]]). The library holds the cookbook but not the Islamic agricultural writers. Abu Mansur names sesame as a crop of Iran in the late tenth century ([[ec11]]).

The densest non-European record: the Tamil press and the Chola lamp-endowments, the Tang calendar, the monastery lamp, the Buddhist ladder, Tang kaymak, ti-hu and fried foreign cakes, and Japan, which bans meat in 675, cooks without oil and takes a milk-skin tribute ([[ec3]], [[b5]], [[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]], [[ec9]], [[e4]], [[o2]], [[e3]], [[ec6]], [[ec8]]).

One entry: the shea record at Kirikongo, Burkina Faso ([[ec7]]). Africa’s fat history in these centuries is far larger than one entry; the library holds no source on Ethiopia, the Sahel’s herders, the Maghreb’s oil or the Swahili coast.

Two entries, each independent of the folio’s own threads: the Birnirk culture hunts seals, caribou and perhaps whale on the Bering Strait, in the same stone-and-clay lamp tradition as the Arctic entries before and after it, and gives rise to the Thule; and the Classic Maya, whose own deer-and-dog diet stayed lean, answer their need for fat with three native oil palms — coyol, huiscoyol and cohune — cultivated outright at Copán, though strangely absent from the otherwise exceptionally preserved village of Cerén ([[ec12]], [[ec13]]).
No entry. Pacific coconut voyages are in an earlier folio, with a placeholder date.

sources.intro: A thin and uneven record: a translated Baghdad cookbook, a translated Frankish extract, South Indian inscriptions, a popular history of butter, Achaya, Needham, Anderson, Chang and Ishige for Asia, and Mueller, Ward and Ellis for Europe; three entries (Japan’s *so*, Spanish oil words, Kirikongo shea) rest on web summaries and one (the Prophet’s oil) on an unsourced anecdote.
main: Nasrallah’s translation of Ibn Sayyar for Baghdad ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[th2]]); the Fordham extract of the Capitulary De Villis ([[o1]]); South Indian Inscriptions vol. 23 ([[b5]]).

Needham and Kieschnick for the Tang entries ([[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]]); Achaya for the Tamil press ([[ec3]]); Khosrova for butter ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]); Ward for soap ([[ec4]]); Ellis for whales ([[ec5]], [[c1]]).
Ishige for Japan ([[o2]], [[e3]]); Anderson and Chang (Schafer’s Tang chapter) for Tang dairy and the foreign cakes ([[ec8]], [[ec9]], [[e4]]).
Mortazavian, in Bedigian’s *Sesame* volume, for Abu Mansur ([[ec11]]).
Anderson and Ishige, read together, for the Tang court’s Turkic ancestry and for why Japan’s meat taboo became permanent.
Wikipedia (citing Gibbon & Ames; Raghavan et al. 2014) for the Birnirk culture ([[ec12]]).
contested: Mueller’s monastic ‘islands of oil’ cite no councils ([[b1]]); his anecdote of the Prophet’s oil names no source ([[b4]]).
The thousand-year-old Irish butter is a museum label as reported ([[ec2]]); the Icelandic sagas postdate the events ([[c1]]).
Spanish oil words show language, not the introduction of the crop ([[th1]]); the Kirikongo and *so* entries rest on abstracts and encyclopedia pages, not the papers ([[ec7]], [[ec6]]).
Birnirk’s own lamp fuel is not named in the source read, and how much whale the culture actually hunted is itself disputed there ([[ec12]]).
gaps: The Islamic agricultural writers are not covered: Watson’s *Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World* (or an alternative) is not held, and Andalusian, Sicilian and Maghrebi (Ifriqiyan) olive oil are missing.

Africa has one entry; nothing on Aksum and Ethiopia’s butter and oilseeds, Nubia, the Sahel’s pastoral fats or the Swahili coast. Central Asia and the steppe, Tibet, Southeast Asia, the Americas (Maya, Andes) and the Pacific have no entry in these centuries; the search for them found no source in the library, and Reid’s book on Southeast Asia, now added, starts at 1450.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.

Twenty-six entries, so read straight through. The *picture by region* counts the 27 entries: Europe 9, Near East 5, Far East 11, Africa 1, Americas 1; none in Oceania or Worldwide. Several dates are ranges for ‘the early Middle Ages’ because the sources do not narrow them. The Far East carries the folio, with Europe second and Africa a single entry.
The next folio is where documents (customs, Lent rules, Geniza ledgers, whale taxes) make fats countable.
before: The last folio ended with fat moving by every channel an empire and its neighbours offered — trade, administration, conquest. This folio is what is left once the empire that built those channels is gone: each world now keeps its own fat its own way, and only a few things still cross between them.
after: The next folio is where documents — customs registers, Lent rulings, Geniza ledgers, whale taxes — start making fat countable again, and the scattered survivals of this folio become an economy.
